{{short description|Coordinate system relative to a torus}}
{{for|the vector fields|Toroidal–poloidal decomposition}}
[[Image:Toroidal coord.png|thumb|right|250px|A diagram depicting the poloidal ({{math|&theta;}}) direction, represented by the red arrow, and the toroidal ({{math|&zeta;}} or {{math|&phi;}}) direction, represented by the blue arrow.]]

The terms '''toroidal''' and '''poloidal''' refer to directions relative to a [[torus]] of reference. They describe a three-dimensional [[coordinate system]] in which the poloidal direction follows a small circular ring around the surface, while the toroidal direction follows a large circular ring around the torus, encircling the central void.

The earliest use of these terms cited by the [[Oxford English Dictionary]] is by [[Walter M. Elsasser]] (1946) in the context of the generation of the [[Earth's magnetic field]] by currents in the core, with "toroidal" being parallel to lines of constant [[latitude]] and "poloidal" being in the direction of the magnetic field (i.e. towards the [[Geomagnetic pole|poles]]).

The OED also records the later usage of these terms in the context of toroidally confined plasmas, as encountered in [[magnetic confinement fusion]]. In the plasma context, the toroidal direction is the long way around the torus, the corresponding coordinate being denoted by {{math|z}} in the slab approximation or {{math|&zeta;}} or {{math|&phi;}} in magnetic coordinates; the poloidal direction is the short way around the torus, the corresponding coordinate being denoted by {{math|y}} in the slab approximation or {{math|&theta;}} in magnetic coordinates. (The third direction, normal to the magnetic surfaces, is often called the "radial direction", denoted by {{math|x}} in the slab approximation and variously {{math|&psi;}}, {{math|&chi;}}, {{math|r}}, {{math|&rho;}}, or {{math|s}} in magnetic coordinates.)

==Example==
As a simple example from the physics of magnetically confined plasmas, consider an axisymmetric system with circular, concentric magnetic flux surfaces of radius <math>r</math> (a crude approximation to the magnetic field geometry in an early [[tokamak]] but topologically equivalent to any toroidal magnetic confinement system with nested flux surfaces) and denote the toroidal angle by <math>\zeta</math> and the poloidal angle by <math>\theta</math>.
Then the toroidal/poloidal coordinate system relates to standard [[Cartesian coordinate system#Cartesian coordinates in three dimensions|Cartesian coordinates]] by these transformation rules:

:<math> x  = (R_0 +r \cos \theta) \cos\zeta </math>
:<math> y  = s_\zeta (R_0 + r \cos \theta) \sin\zeta  </math>
:<math> z  = s_\theta r \sin \theta. </math>

where <math>s_\theta = \pm 1, s_\zeta = \pm 1</math>.

The natural choice [[Torus#Geometry|geometrically]] is to take <math>s_\theta = s_\zeta = +1</math>, giving the toroidal and poloidal directions shown by the arrows in the figure above, but this makes <math>r,\theta,\zeta</math> a left-handed curvilinear coordinate system. As it is usually assumed in setting up [http://www-fusion.ciemat.es/fusionwiki/index.php/Flux_coordinates#Flux_coordinates ''flux coordinates''] for describing magnetically confined plasmas that the set <math>r,\theta,\zeta</math> forms a ''right''-handed coordinate system, <math> \nabla r\cdot\nabla\theta\times\nabla\zeta > 0</math>, we must either reverse the poloidal direction by taking <math>s_\theta = -1, s_\zeta = +1</math>, or reverse the toroidal direction by taking <math>s_\theta = +1, s_\zeta = -1</math>. Both choices are used in the literature.

==Kinematics==

To study single particle motion in toroidally confined plasma devices, velocity and acceleration vectors must be known. Considering the natural choice <math>s_\theta = s_\zeta = +1</math>, the unit vectors of toroidal and poloidal coordinates system <math>\left(r,\theta,\zeta\right)</math> can be expressed as:

: <math>\mathbf{e}_r = \begin{pmatrix}
    \cos\theta \cos\zeta \\
    \cos\theta \sin\zeta \\
    \sin\theta
\end{pmatrix} \quad
\mathbf{e}_\theta = \begin{pmatrix}
    -\sin\theta \cos\zeta \\
    -\sin\theta \sin\zeta \\
    \cos\theta
\end{pmatrix} \quad
\mathbf{e}_\zeta = \begin{pmatrix}
    -\sin\zeta \\
    \cos\zeta \\
    0
\end{pmatrix}</math>

according to Cartesian coordinates. The position vector is expressed as:

: <math> \mathbf{r} = \left( r + R_0 \cos\theta \right) \mathbf{e}_r - R_0 \sin\theta \mathbf{e}_\theta </math>

The velocity vector is then given by:

: <math> \mathbf{\dot{r}} = \dot{r} \mathbf{e}_r + r\dot{\theta} \mathbf{e}_\theta + \dot{\zeta} \left( R_0 + r \cos\theta \right) \mathbf{e}_\zeta </math>

and the acceleration vector is:

: <math>
\begin{align}
\mathbf{\ddot{r}} = {} & \left( \ddot{r} - r \dot{\theta}^2 - r \dot{\zeta}^2 \cos^2\theta - R_0 \dot{\zeta}^2 \cos\theta \right) \mathbf{e}_r \\[5pt]
& {} + \left( 2\dot{r}\dot{\theta} + r\ddot{\theta} + r\dot{\zeta}^2\cos\theta\sin\theta + R_0 \dot{\zeta}^2 \sin\theta \right) \mathbf{e}_\theta \\[5pt]
& {} + \left( 2 \dot{r}\dot{\zeta}\cos\theta - 2 r \dot{\theta}\dot{\zeta} \sin\theta + \ddot{\zeta} \left( R_0 + r\cos\theta \right) \right) \mathbf{e}_\zeta
\end{align}
</math>
